movements.name: The death
movements.window: Friday, the third hour to sunset
movements.question: What do the sources actually report in those hours?
movements.line: Four accounts of the same afternoon. They agree on the execution and the burial; they diverge on the hour, the last words, and the centurion's verdict.

movements.name: The three days
movements.window: Friday evening to Sunday before dawn
movements.question: Where was he?
movements.line: No Gospel narrates the sabbath. The New Testament answers the question elsewhere, in scattered lines, and later writers filled the silence with more.

movements.name: The forty days
movements.question: Who saw him, and where?
movements.line: Reports begin on Sunday and continue through the weeks after. No single source carries the whole sequence, and Acts alone numbers the span as forty days.

movements.name: The ascension
movements.window: The fortieth day, and ten days after
movements.question: How did it end, and what began?
movements.line: Luke ends his Gospel with a departure near Bethany and begins Acts with the view from Olivet. The witnesses return to Jerusalem, and the story turns toward them.

moments.title: Crucified between two others
moments.line: Mark gives the hour. All four place two others beside him.
moments.tension: Mark has him on the cross by the third hour; John still has Pilate giving sentence at about the sixth.

moments.title: Darkness over the land
moments.line: Three hours of it, until the ninth hour.

moments.title: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
moments.line: The opening line of Psalm 22, cried in Aramaic.

moments.title: Seven sayings from the cross
moments.line: Forgiveness, the promise to the criminal, his mother and the disciple, thirst, the cry of dereliction, “it is finished,” and the commending of his spirit.
moments.attestation: No single Gospel records all seven
moments.tension: The traditional seven is a harmony, not a source. Luke carries three, John three, Matthew and Mark one — the same one.

moments.title: The temple curtain torn
moments.line: Torn in two, from the top to the bottom.

moments.title: The earthquake and the opened tombs
moments.line: Rocks split, tombs opened, and bodies of the saints raised — appearing to many after his own resurrection.
moments.tension: No other source mentions it, inside the New Testament or outside it.

moments.title: The centurion's verdict
moments.line: The officer in charge of the execution says something. What he says depends on the source.
moments.tension: Matthew and Mark: “the Son of God.” Luke: “a righteous man.”

moments.title: The spear, the blood and water
moments.line: The soldiers break the legs of the other two, find him already dead, and pierce his side instead.
moments.tension: John alone reports it, and stops the narrative to insist on an eyewitness for it.

moments.title: Joseph of Arimathea asks for the body
moments.line: A member of the council takes the body, wraps it, and lays it in a tomb cut in rock.

moments.title: The women see where he is laid
moments.line: Named women watch the burial and mark the place.

moments.title: The guard and the sealed stone
moments.line: The chief priests ask Pilate to secure the tomb until the third day.
moments.tension: Matthew is also the only Gospel that names the counter-story it answers — that the disciples stole the body.

moments.title: The day no Gospel narrates
moments.line: Luke says the women rested according to the commandment. Then the record goes quiet for a full day.

moments.title: “Today you will be with me in paradise”
moments.line: Said to the criminal beside him; later readers asked how “today” relates to the three-day interval.

moments.title: Three days and three nights in the heart of the earth
moments.line: The sign of Jonah, given before the fact.
moments.tension: Friday evening to Sunday dawn spans parts of three calendar days but two nights; readers usually appeal to inclusive Jewish day-counting.

moments.title: “He went and preached to the spirits in prison”
moments.line: The clearest New Testament statement that something happened while he was dead — and the most argued over.

moments.title: “He also descended into the lower parts of the earth”
moments.line: Paul reads a psalm about ascent, and infers a descent behind it.
moments.tension: “The lower parts of the earth” has been read as the grave, as the underworld, and simply as the earth itself.

moments.title: “Not abandoned to Hades”
moments.line: Peter's Pentecost sermon applies Psalm 16 to him: his soul was not left in Hades, nor his flesh left to decay.

moments.title: “I have the keys of Death and of Hades”
moments.line: Said by the risen Christ in the opening vision of Revelation.

moments.title: “Who will descend into the abyss?”
moments.line: Paul's rhetorical question — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.

moments.title: The stone is already moved
moments.line: Every account arrives at a tomb that is already open.
moments.tension: No source in the New Testament describes the rising itself. Not one.

moments.title: Someone is waiting at the tomb
moments.line: A figure, or two, tells the women he is not there.
moments.tension: Matthew has an angel and Mark a young man — one figure. Luke has two men, John two angels.

moments.title: The list Paul says he received
moments.line: Died, buried, raised on the third day, appeared — to Cephas, the twelve, five hundred, James, all the apostles, and last of all to Paul.
moments.tension: Paul calls it handed-on material, which puts the formula earlier than the letter carrying it.

moments.title: He eats with them
moments.line: Broiled fish in the room, bread and fish on the shore, and Peter later making a point of the shared meals.

moments.title: Some of them still doubted
moments.line: Matthew puts it in the same sentence as the worship, and does not resolve it.

moments.title: The number comes from one source
moments.line: Acts alone gives the span, and says he spoke of the kingdom of God through it.

moments.title: Led out as far as Bethany
moments.line: He lifts his hands, blesses them, and is parted from them.

moments.title: Taken up, and a cloud received him
moments.line: They are still watching when the cloud takes him out of sight.

moments.title: “Why do you stand looking into the sky?”
moments.line: Two men in white ask the question, and promise a return in the same manner.

moments.title: They walk back from Olivet
moments.line: A sabbath day's journey from the city — the one geographic detail given.

moments.title: Mark's one-line ascension
moments.line: Received up into heaven, and seated at the right hand of God.
moments.tension: These verses are absent from the earliest complete manuscripts of Mark.

moments.title: What starts next
moments.line: The record stops following him and starts following them.

appearances.line: She takes him for the gardener until he says her name.
appearances.note: Mark's notice belongs to the longer ending.

appearances.who: The women returning from the tomb
appearances.where: On the road back to the city
appearances.line: He meets them as they run to tell the others.
Two sources report it. Neither narrates it.
He walks with them unrecognized, and they know him when he breaks the bread.

appearances.who: The eleven and those with them
appearances.line: He shows them his hands and side, and asks for something to eat.
He offers Thomas the evidence Thomas asked for.
A night of empty nets, then breakfast on the shore.

appearances.who: More than five hundred at once
appearances.line: The largest reported appearance, and the least described.
appearances.note: Paul adds that most were still alive when he wrote — an invitation to go and ask.

appearances.line: Named on his own in the earliest list, and nowhere else.
A second group sighting, distinct from the twelve.
The commission — and the note that some doubted.
Acts summarizes the whole span rather than listing sightings.
He puts his own sighting on the same list, and calls it last of all.
appearances.note: Different in kind from the rest — after the ascension, and by his own account out of due time.

descent.name: Ignatius, To the Magnesians
descent.claim: The prophets waited for him as their teacher, and when he came he raised them from the dead.
descent.establishes: A bishop writing within roughly eighty years of the crucifixion already assumes he did something for the righteous dead. It is the earliest surviving trace of the idea.
descent.limits: One clause inside a letter about church unity. It assumes the idea rather than reporting an event.

descent.name: Odes of Solomon 42
descent.claim: He goes down to Sheol; the dead run to him, ask to be led out, and he sets his name upon their heads.
descent.establishes: The oldest surviving collection of Christian hymns puts the descent in the first person and sings it as rescue.
descent.limits: Poetry, and its date, language of origin, and community are all disputed. It shows what was sung, not what was witnessed.

descent.name: The Ascension of Isaiah
descent.claim: The Beloved descends through the seven heavens unrecognized, taking the form of each as he passes, and afterwards rises with every heaven watching.
descent.establishes: An early Christian picture in which the going-down and the going-up are one movement rather than two events.
descent.limits: A vision, not a report. Its Christian chapters are debated in date, and it was never received as scripture.

descent.name: The Gospel of Peter
descent.claim: Two figures whose heads reach heaven bring him out of the tomb, the cross follows them, and a voice from heaven asks whether he preached to those who sleep. The cross answers yes.
descent.establishes: That by the second century a Christian narrative already had him preaching to the dead — and that someone was willing to narrate the exit from the tomb.
descent.limits: A single fragment, recovered at Akhmim in 1886 in a copy centuries later than the text. It was not received as scripture, and its passion narrative departs from all four Gospels.

descent.name: Epistula Apostolorum
descent.claim: The risen Christ answers the apostles' questions directly, including what he did for those who had already died.
descent.establishes: That the forty days were being filled in with dialogue within a century, by writers who felt the Gospels had left the period thin.
descent.limits: Written to teach, in the voice of the risen Christ. Read it as second-century theology, not as testimony to the forty days.

descent.name: The Descent into Hell (Gospel of Nicodemus)
descent.claim: Two sons of Simeon return from the dead to testify: the gates of Hades broken, Adam and the patriarchs led out, and Hades arguing with Satan over who let him in.
descent.establishes: The fullest developed form of the harrowing, and the direct source of most later art, drama, and hymnody about it.
descent.limits: Centuries after the events, with no independent witness behind it. It records what Christians came to picture, not what anyone reported.

descent.name: The “descended” clause in the creed
descent.establishes: That by the late fourth century some Latin churches confessed a descent as part of the baptismal creed. Rufinus of Aquileia, writing around AD 404, notes the clause in his own church's creed and observes that the Roman form does not carry it.
descent.limits: A creed records what a church confessed, not a source for what happened. The clause is later than the New Testament lines it summarizes, and churches have never agreed on what it means.

outsideCanon.name: The Gospel of Peter
outsideCanon.survives: Fragmentary Greek witnesses. The principal passion-and-resurrection copy is centuries later than the proposed composition.
outsideCanon.claim: Soldiers guard the tomb and witness two immense figures bringing out a third, followed by a cross that answers a voice from heaven. The women arrive afterward and find the tomb open.
outsideCanon.establishes: By the second century, at least one Christian retelling made the resurrection itself visible and expanded the guarded-tomb tradition dramatically.
outsideCanon.limits: The work is fragmentary, later than the New Testament sources, and its literary relationship to the canonical Gospels is debated. It is not another eyewitness report.

outsideCanon.name: The Epistle of the Apostles
outsideCanon.date: 2nd century, often placed in its later decades
outsideCanon.survives: A fragmentary Coptic codex from the 4th or 5th century, a Latin palimpsest, and a complete text in later Ethiopic manuscripts.
outsideCanon.claim: The eleven present an extended dialogue with the resurrected Christ about resurrection, judgment, Gentiles, false teaching, and Paul, continuing until a final ascension scene.
outsideCanon.establishes: A second-century writer used the forty-day gap as a setting for instruction and defended a particular version of apostolic teaching in the apostles' collective voice.
outsideCanon.limits: The work draws on earlier Jesus traditions and speaks pseudonymously. It records second-century theology and church conflict, not an additional first-generation appearance account.

outsideCanon.name: The Apocryphon of James
outsideCanon.survives: One damaged Coptic copy in the 4th-century Nag Hammadi Codex I.
outsideCanon.claim: Jesus singles out James and Peter for private post-resurrection teaching about suffering, the kingdom, and understanding. His departure becomes an ascension sequence.
outsideCanon.establishes: Later Christians placed competing claims about authority and suffering into private conversations between the risen Jesus and favored disciples.
outsideCanon.limits: Its author is unknown, the identity of James is ambiguous, and only one later manuscript survives. It cannot supply an independent itinerary of appearances.

outsideCanon.name: The Gospel of Mary
outsideCanon.survives: Two 3rd-century Greek fragments and a 4th- or 5th-century Coptic copy. Less than half of the work survives, and its opening is lost.
outsideCanon.claim: The preserved text closes a dialogue with Jesus, then presents Mary's vision and her disputed teaching. Peter and Andrew challenge her; Levi defends her.
outsideCanon.establishes: The risen-Jesus setting could authorize Mary's teaching and expose arguments over who understood Jesus and who was permitted to speak for him.
outsideCanon.limits: The lost opening probably contained the appearance, but that scene is not preserved. The surviving work is theological dialogue, not a recoverable event sequence.

outsideCanon.name: The Wisdom of Jesus Christ
outsideCanon.date: Date disputed: late 1st or early 2nd century to the 3rd
outsideCanon.survives: Greek and Coptic witnesses copied in the 4th and 5th centuries.
outsideCanon.claim: Disciples and women gather on a mountain in Galilee after the resurrection. The Savior appears and answers thirteen rounds of questions about the universe, divine powers, mortality, and salvation.
outsideCanon.establishes: Matthew's Galilean mountain became a reusable setting for later cosmological teaching delivered by an appearing Savior.
outsideCanon.limits: The work reshapes material from Eugnostos the Blessed, and its date is unusually disputed. Its scene functions as a literary frame for theology rather than an event report.

outsideCanon.name: The Letter of Peter to Philip
outsideCanon.date: Late 2nd to early 3rd century, often proposed
outsideCanon.survives: Two broadly comparable 4th-century Coptic copies, in Nag Hammadi Codex VIII and Codex Tchacos.
outsideCanon.claim: The reunited disciples gather on the Mount of Olives. Jesus appears as a great light and voice, answers questions, ascends, and commissions them before they return to Jerusalem.
outsideCanon.establishes: A later community rewrote the Olivet and Pentecost pattern around unity, persecution, cosmic powers, and Peter's leadership.
outsideCanon.limits: The scene echoes Acts while serving a distinct theological system. Its two later manuscripts preserve reception history, not independent evidence for the ascension.

outsideCanon.name: The Questions of Bartholomew
outsideCanon.date: 2nd to 4th century; composition and development debated
outsideCanon.survives: Several divergent language versions. The principal Greek manuscripts are medieval, copied from the 13th to 15th centuries.
outsideCanon.claim: Bartholomew questions Jesus about the crucifixion, the descent to Hades, heaven, the abyss, and Satan. Some versions place the exchange after the resurrection; one places it before.
outsideCanon.establishes: The unanswered interval and the authority of Bartholomew became a framework for increasingly elaborate explanations of Hades and the unseen world.
outsideCanon.limits: Its versions disagree even about when the dialogue occurs, and the surviving copies are late. It is evidence for a developing tradition, not a stable early narrative.

outsideCanon.name: Pistis Sophia
outsideCanon.date: 2nd- and 3rd-century layers have been proposed; composite
outsideCanon.survives: One Sahidic Coptic manuscript, the Askew Codex, copied around AD 250-300.
outsideCanon.claim: Its main frame says Jesus taught the disciples for eleven years after the resurrection before revealing higher mysteries. Another section returns to a Galilean mountain immediately after the resurrection.
outsideCanon.establishes: The post-resurrection period could be expanded almost without limit and used to authorize a large body of ritual, cosmological, and salvific teaching.
outsideCanon.limits: The work is internally inconsistent and appears to compile multiple texts. Its eleven-year setting belongs to a later theological world, not the chronology of Acts.

questions.question: Does the earliest Gospel have a resurrection appearance?
questions.answer: As we have it in the oldest complete manuscripts, no. Mark ends at 16:8 with the women running from the tomb, afraid, saying nothing to anyone. The twelve verses that follow — the appearances, the ascension, the signs — are absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and read in a different style. Most printed Bibles carry them with a note. This room marks them wherever they are used.

questions.question: Galilee, or Jerusalem?
questions.answer: Matthew and Mark send the disciples north to Galilee, and Matthew's climax happens on a mountain there. Luke keeps them in and around Jerusalem and has them told to stay in the city. Both cannot be the whole picture; harmonies exist, but they are readings, not sources.

questions.question: One messenger at the tomb, or two?
questions.answer: Matthew has an angel and Mark a young man in white — one figure. Luke has two men in dazzling clothing, John two angels seated where the body had been. Some readers harmonize this by saying one writer mentions only the speaker; others treat it as variation in retelling. The sources themselves do not explain the difference.

questions.question: The same day, or forty days later?
questions.answer: Luke 24 reads as one continuous day that ends with the ascension at Bethany. Acts 1 — the same author, writing to the same reader — gives forty days. Luke's Gospel compresses; Acts spells it out. The forty-day figure rests on that one verse.

questions.question: Why are the women missing from the earliest list?
questions.answer: Paul's list is the earliest written account of the appearances, and it begins with Cephas. The women, who come first in all four Gospels, are not in it. Readers have explained this by the conventions of a formal witness list; the plain fact is that the earliest source omits the first witnesses, and the later sources put them first anyway.

questions.question: Did anyone claim to see the rising itself?
questions.answer: No New Testament source does. Every account begins at a tomb that is already open. The first text to narrate the exit is the Gospel of Peter, in the second century, and it is not a witness — it is a story written later, by someone filling the same gap everyone else felt.
